But. if the goal is to scare people away. from crime by publicly displaying death. , is that really effective? Based on. current research, it likely is not. The. U.S. National Research Council reviewed. decades of related studies and. concluded that existing research cannot. prove whether the death penalty. increases, decreases, or has no effect. on murder rates. Research institutions. under the Department of Justice have. also pointed out that what truly serves. as a deterrent is the likelihood of. being caught, not the severity of the. punishment. July found that 59%believe it does not. deter serious crime. Some former. officials also worry that a livestream. would package Hassan as a martyr,. serving as a recruitment tool. Moreover. , history has shown that public. executions do not necessarily produce. the results governments expect. During. early public executions in the U.S.,. people would even bring picnics to. watch; it only made people numb to. violence and emboldened criminals,. which is why states began moving. executions into prisons starting in the. 1820s. If public executions could. really deter crime, why were they moved. inside prisons in the first place? Looking back at Taiwan, our death. penalty is carried out by firing squad. within detention centers, and it is not. open to the public. As mentioned. earlier, nearly 60%of Americans believe. the death penalty cannot deter serious. crime, but polls in Taiwan show about. 80%of the public supports it, with many. believing it can deter crime and. maintain order. There is a significant. gap here compared to American public. opinion, so I’d like to ask: what is. your main reason for supporting the. death penalty? Is it because you. believe those who commit heinous crimes. should pay the price, or because you. believe the death penalty truly deters. crime? 摘要

八旬老婦遭驅離逝世引爆全國怒火

作者指出，西班牙馬德里一位87歲的老婦人瑪麗．卡門（Mari Carmen）在同一間公寓生活了長達70年且按時繳租，卻因法規修改面臨強制遷離。歷經多年訴訟與抗爭後，她在第四次驅逐行動中被擔架抬上救護車送醫，不久後在醫院過世。這場悲劇引爆西班牙全國性的強烈抗議，抗議者佔領太陽門廣場要求政府立法禁止在無安置方案下驅逐房客，更促使首相解散國會提前大選。

歷史遺留的「舊租約」與法律角力

作者回溯源頭，瑪麗．卡門自1956年佛朗哥獨裁時期便與父母入住，合約屬於早期受法律保障、租金極低且可世代繼承的「舊租約」。然而，1994年西班牙修法限制繼承次數與期限。當公寓產權於近年轉賣給不動產公司後，新房東要求調漲至她無法負擔的租金並提起訴訟。法院最終判定繼承期限已過而判房東勝訴，儘管各方在悲劇發生前夕曾達成協議讓她以原本租金重返公寓，但她已來不及回家。

作者進一步探討民眾憤怒背後的深層住房危機。首先是薪資完全追不上房價，過去十年間工資僅成長30%，房價與租金漲幅卻高達80%以上，單身租客租金甚至吃掉過半收入；其次是供給嚴重不足，2008年金融海嘯後營建業萎縮，加上社會住宅比例僅佔約1.5%至1.7%，遠低於歐盟平均，預估至2028年將面臨高達百萬戶的住宅缺口。

The housing crisis we are discussing. today isn't in Taiwan, it's in Spain,. but I believe everyone will find it. very relatable. The. grandmother was eventually carried out. on a stretcher to an ambulance and. taken to the hospital, where she passed. away shortly after, never being able to. return to the home she had lived in for. most of her life. What exactly did the. grandmother do wrong? Actually, nothing. at all. The problem stemmed from a. lease her father signed 70 years ago,. combined with subsequent revisions to. rental laws. What was initially just a. legal dispute between a landlord and a. tenant unexpectedly ignited outrage. across all of Spain. Large crowds took. to the streets to seek justice for the. grandmother, demanding that the. government protect the right to housing. , while parliament argued intensely. over housing policy, eventually leading. the Prime Minister to dissolve. parliament and call for early elections. . Hello. Everyone, I am Fan Chi,. welcome to "Fan Looks at the World." This story begins in 1956. According to. El País, Spain was still under the. dictatorship of Franco at that time. The then 17-year-old Mari Carmen moved. into an apartment in Madrid with her. parents. Her father passed away in 1960. , and the lease was transferred to her. mother. In 2005, her mother also passed. away, and the lease was then inherited. by Mari Carmen. This system is known as. the "old lease," and it has several.

specific characteristics. Simply put,. these were rental contracts protected. by law in the early days; not only was. the rent far below market rates, but. under certain conditions, family. members could inherit the lease, and. landlords could not refuse. According. to BBC, the rent Mari Carmen inherited. was 500 euros, which is nearly 18,000. New Taiwan Dollars at the current. exchange rate, while her monthly. pension was 1,350 euros, or about. 48,000 New Taiwan Dollars, which was. initially affordable. The problem arose. in 2018 when the owner's family sold. the entire building to a real estate. company. The company offered to sell. the apartment to Mari Carmen for 8.8. million New Taiwan Dollars and asked if. she wanted to buy it. However, the. elderly lady was too old to obtain a. mortgage, and she had no relatives to. act as guarantors. Later, the company. sold the apartment to another real. estate firm. This company initially. demanded rent......that was nearly. double her pension. They later offered. a discount, but it was still 300 euros. higher than her monthly pension, which. is nearly 10,000 New Taiwan Dollars; even if she didn't eat or drink, she. still couldn't afford it. Then, in 2020. , the company filed a lawsuit, claiming. that the old lease Mari Carmen. inherited was no longer valid. This. brings us to the Spanish rental law. amended in 1994. Previously, old rental. contracts could be passed down through. generations, but the new law began. limiting the number of successions and. their duration. Like Maria Carmen,. whose father passed the lease to her. mother, and then her mother passed it.

to her, this represents a second. succession. Under current regulations,. an adult child like her can generally. only remain for two more years. The. legal battle then began. The second-instance court ruled that. even if the landlord had continued to. collect rent for years, it did not. override the legal time limits on old. contracts, thus overturning the verdict. in favor of the landlord. Later, the. Supreme Court did not accept Maria. Carmen’s appeal, and the ruling. became final. During these years of. litigation, tenant unions and neighbors. joined in to help. Over the past year,. three eviction attempts were delayed. due to protests, but on September 23rd. of this year, the fourth eviction. finally arrived. Large crowds gathered. outside the apartment that day; police. cordoned off the area while court. officials entered to carry out the. eviction. Spain via television and the internet,. causing a national outcry, as many. citizens felt deeply for the elderly. woman’s plight. The situation drew. immense sympathy. Following the. eviction, hundreds of people. spontaneously went to Madrid's landmark. "Puerta del Sol" that weekend to set up. tents, demanding the government pass a. "Maria Carmen Law" to ban evictions.

without providing alternative housing,. and tents began to spring up everywhere. , spreading rapidly. It escalated. quickly. The reason people are this. angry is that Spain’s housing crisis. is becoming increasingly severe. There. are several problems; first, wages. cannot keep up with housing prices. During the 2008 financial crisis, Spain. experienced a property bubble burst and. skyrocketing unemployment. Despite the. later economic recovery, salaries have. completely failed to keep pace with. soaring housing costs. According to El. País statistics, over the decade from. 2015 to 2025, Spanish wages grew by. only 30%, while the cost of home. purchases rose by 80%and rents surged. by 87%. Furthermore, the economy. is overly reliant on low-wage tourism. and service industries, leaving the. working class helpless against high. housing prices. Second, there is a. severe shortage of housing supply. Before the market crash, Spain could. build 600,000 new homes a year. the EU average of 6%to 7%. This is. because past policies over-encouraged. home ownership, with most units sold. off directly rather than kept for. long-term government rentals. This twisted ecosystem is. ruthlessly stripping local residents of. their basic right to housing. The. accumulation of these problems has led. to a situation where, although 73%of. Spaniards own their homes, over 60%of. young people aged 18 to 34 still live.

with their parents. Back to the case of. Mari Carmen. On September 28th, with. mediation from the Madrid city. government, both parties reached an. agreement to sign a new eight-year. lease. October 6th and moved the general. election forward to November 29th,. letting voters directly decide the. future of Spain's housing policy. The. apartment she rents is located here, in. an upscale residential area of Madrid. It's next to the famous Retiro Park,. with the Prado Museum to the west and. 摘要

惡魔即將回歸：金槿植案引發南韓社會集體焦慮

作者指出，南韓近期因重大兒少性侵犯金槿植即將刑滿獲釋，引發廣大家長與社區居民的極度恐慌。金槿植曾於2006年間誘拐並性侵11名未成年人，年紀最小的被害人僅9歲。原定於2022年出獄的他，因檢方即時查出其於2002年的懸案並涉及獄中施暴，獲法院追加刑期延至2027年釋放。然而，法院駁回了檢方對其施以化學去勢的聲請，僅命其配戴電子腳鐐十年，使大眾深感不安，深怕這顆「定時炸彈」再次危害社區。

借鑑美國經驗：南韓版「潔西卡法」重回輿論焦點

面對大眾恐慌，南韓再度激起制定「潔西卡法案」（Jessica\'s Law）的呼聲。作者說明，該法源於美國佛州一名九歲女童潔西卡遭三級性侵累犯殺害的慘劇，促使美國各州立法嚴格限制性侵犯出獄後的居住範圍。南韓雖然設有性犯罪者資訊公開系統，但過往如趙斗淳、朴炳化等連環性侵犯出獄後租屋於校園或住宅區附近，屢次引爆住戶抗議與恐慌。南韓法務部因此提出《高風險性犯罪者指定居住法案》，擬強制將高風險性侵犯集中安置於國家設立的隔離設施中。

安全與人權的拉鋸：指定居住法案的爭議與流局

法案提出後引發各界正反激辯。贊成方主張，高風險性犯罪者的再犯率高，保護兒少安全是國家的底線，現行電子腳鐐防不勝防，必須透過集中管理與性衝動抑制治療來防範再犯。反對方則質疑，服刑完畢後強制收容有違憲與雙重處罰之嫌，嚴重侵犯居住遷徙自由；且設施選址面臨嚴重的鄰避效應（NIMBY），若長期全面隔離，恐讓受刑人更趨反社會，治標不治本。這項法案最終因違憲爭議與地方抗拒，於2024年5月國會任期結束時自動廢案。

制度的借鏡與反思：密集監管代替絕對隔離

作者最後借鏡台灣現況指出，台灣與南韓同樣面臨人口稠密的問題，若對更生人施加極端的生活空間限制，往往會將其逼入絕境，因無法謀生或憤恨而更容易重蹈覆轍。因此，台灣的《性侵害犯罪防治法》目前採取密集監控與身心治療輔導，而非採取絕對的空間隔離設施，試圖在防範犯罪再發與維持社會復歸機能之間尋求務實的平衡。

Recently, a group of parents in South. Korea has fallen into a state of. collective panic because of a man about. to be released from prison. His name is. Kim Geun-sik. Back in 2000, he had. already built a criminal record for. sexually assaulting minors. Not long. after his release in 2006, he targeted. school zones and quiet residential. areas, exploiting children's sympathy. by asking them to help an "uncle" move. heavy objects, eventually abducting and. sexually assaulting 11 innocent minors. The youngest victim was only nine years. old. Now, this dangerous individual. with a history of recidivism is about. to be released back into society. Under. current South Korean law, he could. legally rent the house right next to. yours and watch your children go to. school every day. When someone with a. history of harming so many children. regains their freedom, do we actually. have the right to demand the government. keep these people permanently... isolated? Hello everyone, I am Fan Qi. Welcome to "Fan's World." Kim Geun-sik. originally completed his 15-year prison. sentence in 2022, but the news of his. impending release threw all of South. Korean society into anxiety. Residents. in his hometown and the community where. he was rumored to be moving upon. release were so angry that they. surrounded government buildings in. protest, with some parents even saying. they would move away overnight with. their children. On the eve of his. release, prosecutors uncovered a cold. case from 2002 involving a child sex. crime for which he had never been. charged. Coupled with his involvement. in a violent assault while in prison,. the court quickly ruled to re-detain. him, temporarily calming the public. panic. Ultimately, following a ruling.

by the Supreme Court of South Korea,. Kim Geun-sik was given an additional. five-year sentence, delaying his. release date. It was pushed to 2027,. but 2027 is just around the corner, and. this ticking time bomb will eventually. be released back into society. The. prosecution had strongly urged the. court to mandate chemical castration. for someone as remorseless and. dangerous as Kim to suppress his. criminal impulses. However, the court. rejected the request, citing the fact. that he had already been sentenced to. long-term imprisonment and would be. required to wear an electronic ankle. monitor for ten years, arguing there. was still room for his rehabilitation. Once the verdict was out, most South. Korean parents found it hard to accept. A serial predator who harmed over a. dozen children can not only freely. choose where to live after his release,. but isn't even subject to physiological. drug control—how are ordinary people. supposed to live? This has brought a. long-debated bill in South Korea back. to the forefront: the High-Risk Sex. Offender Residence Restriction Act,. known as the "Korean Jessica's Law." Jessica’s Law stems from a child. sexual assault and murder case in. Florida 25 years ago. The victim,. nine-year-old Jessica, was kidnapped. from her home in the middle of the. night. Her body was found days later in. a nearby pit, and forensic evidence. confirmed she had been sexually. assaulted and buried alive. What made. the case even more unacceptable was. that the killer, Lundy, was already a. registered Tier 3 sex offender. This is. the highest level in the U.S. sex. offender registry, requiring lifetime. registration and in-person check-ins. every three months. He lived just over.

100 meters away from Jessica’s home. Jessica’s father launched a national. campaign demanding legislative reform. Consequently, U.S. states began passing. Jessica’s Laws, strictly restricting. where such child sex offenders could. live after release. For example, the. California version prohibits offenders. from living within 2,000 feet of. schools, parks, and other places where. children gather, while also requiring. lifetime monitoring. So, why is South. Korea......starting to discuss whether. to push for this bill again now? This. has a lot to do with South Korea’s. sex offender notification system. South. Korean citizens can use their ID. numbers to check the website for. registered sex offenders in their area,. including their photos, criminal. records, and places of residence. The. duration of this public disclosure is. determined by court orders. While this. was originally intended to safeguard. the public's right to know, the more. people know, the more it has become a. major source of fear for parents. Even. more unsettling is that this personal. information is typically only disclosed. for five years, meaning some criminals. can simply "disappear" once that period. ends. High-profile cases that have. received intense media attention in. recent years have pushed public anxiety. to its peak, such as Cho Doo-soon, whom. we previously reported on, and the 2022. Suwon serial sex offender Park. Byung-hwa. Both sparked social panic. upon their release. Take Park Byung-hwa. as an example: when his family helped. him find a place to stay, they. intentionally hid his identity to sign. a lease and moved in near the back gate. of Suwon University. The unsuspecting. landlord only realized a serial sex. offender was living in his property.

after watching the news. He immediately. issued a formal notice citing contract. fraud and demanded that he move out. immediately. This incident not only. left the female students at Suwon. University, right next door......in a. state of panic, but local residents. also took to the streets in protest,. demanding this monster be driven out of. their city. The entire society has. reached a point where every time an. offender is released, the whole. community is thrown into chaos. In 2023. , the South Korean Ministry of Justice. initially proposed a bill modeled after. the U.S., aiming to ban high-risk. offenders from living within 500 meters. of schools. However, due to South. Korea's high population density, such a. strict rule would leave almost no legal. land in Seoul, forcing offenders into. remote areas, which would be unfair to. residents there. Later, during a. cabinet meeting on January 2, 2024, the. South Korean government passed an. amendment renamed the "High-Risk Sex. Offender Residence Designation Act." It. abolished the distance restriction and. mandated that high-risk sex offenders. be required to reside in state-run. isolation facilities upon their release. from prison. It sounds straightforward,. but this bill has sparked an intense. debate. Proponents argue that, first,. the recidivism rate for high-risk sex. offenders is as high as 13%, with 26%of. victims being children under 13. Protecting vulnerable children is a. national baseline, and the right to. safety of ordinary citizens outweighs. the offenders 'freedom of movement. Second, the current electronic anklet. system is ineffective, with several. cases of offenders removing them to. flee or even commit murder in recent. years. Instead of leaving them as.

ticking time bombs in communities, it. is better to manage them in centralized. facilities. Third, the Ministry of. Justice reports that since the sex. drive suppression treatment program. began in 2011, only one person among. those treated has reoffended—a rate. of just 1.3%, far lower than the 10%for. those untreated. This shows that. proactive measures are necessary; combining physical isolation with. medication is essential to curb. recidivism. However. On the other hand,. the opposition has raised different. concerns. First, there are serious. concerns about the law being. unconstitutional. Once prisoners have. served their court-mandated sentences,. they are free citizens. Forced house. arrest by the state severely violates. the freedom of residence and movement. guaranteed by the constitution. We are. talking about sex offenders now, but. what about serial killers next? Once. this line is crossed, there will be. endless excuses for the state to expand. its power. Second, isolation facilities. will trigger an extreme "Not In My. Backyard"(NIMBY) effect. Everyone. agrees on centralized management, but. where should the facilities be built? Should they be in downtown Seoul or. remote towns? Shifting the burden of. public safety onto specific areas. causes concern that those neighborhoods. will face decline, leading to regional. conflict, and ultimately, ensuring that. no suitable location can ever be found. Third, it treats the symptoms but not. the root cause. Residency restrictions. have time limits; after 10 or 15 years,. they must return to general society. If. they develop more antisocial tendencies. within facilities of complete isolation. , could they become an even more. dangerous ticking time bomb when.

released? The bill faced strong. objections from South Korea's legal. community. Mandatory confinement raises. concerns about "double jeopardy" and. crosses the red line of freedom of. residence and movement protected by the. constitution. Localities have also. fought over where to build these. facilities; no one wants this hot. potato, leading the bill to expire. automatically when the National. Assembly term ended in May 2024. Even. if a new National Assembly proposes it. again, as long as the two major. obstacles of constitutionality and. electoral controversy remain unresolved. , the bill will stay stuck in. parliament, unable to complete the. legislative process. Looking at Taiwan,. there are currently no strict. regulations on residency distance, nor. requirements for mandatory placement in. specific facilities. The reason is. similar to South Korea: Taiwan is also. densely populated. Past experience. tells us that if they are pushed into a. corner with no way out, unable to find. work or housing, they are more likely. to return to a path of crime out of a. need for survival or pure anger. Therefore, Taiwan's Sexual Assault. Crime Prevention Act utilizes intensive. monitoring and treatment to replace. absolute spatial isolation, such as. mandatory electronic anklets, nighttime. curfews, regular compulsory. psychological therapy, and reporting to. police stations. Regarding information. disclosure, South Korea puts the data. in the public eye, which amounts to the. "social death" of the offender. While. Taiwan allows inquiries, the threshold. is relatively high; one must provide. legitimate reasons to local police. For. example, if you are a kindergarten. director, you must verify the.

employee's background through an. investigation before you are permitted. to conduct a search. Experts believe. that extreme social exclusion is often. the final straw that drives them to. give up on themselves and reoffend. Taiwan's design seeks to strike a. balance between protecting the public's. right to know and assisting offenders. in reintegrating into society. Traditional penal concepts assume that. the longer criminals are locked away,. the better, "out of sight, out of mind. " However, it is regrettable that no. law can provide society with an. environment that is absolutely free of. danger. Unless they are sentenced to. death or life imprisonment, they will. one day return to the spaces where you. and I live. Thus, the controversy over.
